entries.note: From a Scottish Gaelic or Irish word for a domesticated animal; the earliest Scottish uses in the 16th–17th centuries meant a hand-reared lamb, as in Johnson's dictionary.
Stroking an animal, a sense from the 1600s that comes from the noun [[pet]]; British 'no heavy petting' pool signs meant no snogging.
An animal abandoned by its mother and reared by hand; used almost interchangeably with [[pet]] for lambs.
An ironic use of [[pet]] meaning 'favourite': your absolute favourite worst thing.
Reflects the older sense of [[pet]] as an indulged, spoilt child, quoted from 1788, which implies favouritism.
Origin unknown; one of a puzzling set with [[frog]], [[hog]], [[pig]] and [[stag]] that had an Old English double G, probably starting as cutesy diminutives that replaced [[hound]].
Like [[dog]], probably began as a cute diminutive and replaced the older word frosh, which German speakers will recognise.
Like [[dog]], probably a cutesy diminutive that became the generic word, replacing the older [[swine]].
Borrowed from English [[dog]], like similar words in other languages; it usually means a mastiff, probably because Britain's best-known exported dog was the [[mastiff]].
Once the generic word for dogs; it swapped places with [[dog]] and became the more specific, breed-focused term.
A dog breed whose name means 'dwarf dog' in Welsh.
From German Dachs 'badger' plus hound; the dogs were bred to chase badgers out of their holes.
The Old French source meant 'great [[cur]]' and came originally from a Latin word meaning tame or gentle.
A 13th-century word for a dog, almost always a badly behaved or ill-bred one; supposedly from a root meaning 'growl'.
From Middle English 'fisting [[cur]]' (farting dog); it first described lively little dogs, supposedly because ladies blamed their farts on their lapdogs.
A Japanese breed name, perhaps after the brushwood landscape where it hunted or its golden coat.
Said to be an ancient Sumerian word meaning 'plunge earth', supposedly because the dogs leapt off camels' backs during hunts.
From German Pudelhund, named after puddles because they were bred as water dogs with quick-drying curly coats.
A misleading breed name: neither Australian Shepherds nor mini Aussies are Australian, so Jess's mini American Shepherd is the accurate name.
From French poupée 'doll', related to puppet and [[poppet]], since little dogs were playthings; it replaced [[whelp]].
A term of endearment related to [[puppy]] and puppet; Rob wonders whether Americans use it.
The earlier word for baby dogs, later replaced by [[puppy]].
From the Book of St Albans, the first written use of 'litter' as a collective noun for [[whelp|puppies]]; its collective nouns were often tongue-in-cheek.
Another collective noun found in the Book of St Albans alongside [[litter of whelps]].
Probably a variation on French chaton, 'little cat', from chat.
Similar words appear across many European language families, probably arising independently like [[meow]]; Late Latin cattus may come from a North African word, as Nubian and Berber show.
Many languages have similar words because they each imitate the sound, not because they borrowed it; the same reasoning is applied to [[cat]].
An imitative sound used to call a cat, like [[meow]].
From felis, the classical Latin word for cat, which is older than the Late Latin cattus behind [[cat]].
From Attabi, a striped silk cloth made in Baghdad's Attabi district; once imported to England, its wavy striped pattern gave the cat its name.
German word for a male cat that also means a hangover; the hosts don't know why, which leads them to [[hair of the dog that bit you]].

entries.term: hair of the dog that bit you
entries.note: Its earliest 16th-century uses mean drinking alcohol for a hangover, not treating dog bites, so the dog-bite cure was probably figurative from the start.
In Old English it meant the turtle dove, imitating its cooing; in the 1600s French tortue was misheard as turtle and applied to the reptile, once called marine [[tortoise|tortoises]].
The order that includes all [[turtle|turtles]], tortoises and terrapins, from Latin testa 'shell'.
Now means land-dwelling turtles; from Middle English tortuse, spelling influenced by porpoise, from Latin 'twisted' (feet shape) or Tartarus, the abyss below Hades.
Probably related to [[bovine]]; Pliny described a giant mythical snake that drank cows' milk, and Linnaeus later applied boa constrictor (1758) to a South American snake.
Named after the lizard's noisy call, probably through a Malay or Javanese imitation of the sound.
Probably Persian, meaning 'inside flame', from the myth that salamanders were born in fire because they crawled from burning rotten logs; heraldic ones look dragon-like.
An Aztec word, from Nahuatl.
Means 'ground lion', covered in an earlier episode; the hosts joke that the eyes and colour change are more distinctive than anything lion-like.
The French word for [[bat]], meaning 'bald mouse'; Rob thinks 'flying mouse' would fit better.
An old word for a [[bat]] that the hosts prefer to [[chauve-souris]].
Covered in an earlier episode; it means the same thing as flutter, like [[flittermouse]].
From Old High German hamustro, from Russian, ultimately Iranian: Avestan hamaestar means 'one who tramples down', probably because they destroyed crops and food stores.
Means hoarding, buying more than you need like a [[hamster]] storing food in its cheeks; German also has a verb meaning to hoard, and the term surged during the pandemic.
The collective noun for hamsters, 'horde' meaning an army rather than hoarding, which fits [[hamster]]'s 'trampler' meaning.
What English speakers called the [[hamster]] before the word 'hamster' was adopted.
Neither from Guinea nor a pig: maybe named for pig-like shape and noises, or the guinea hog, with Guinea meaning any far-off land or slave-ship cargo.
Actually does come from Guinea, unlike the [[guinea pig]]; guinea fowls were originally called [[turkey|turkeys]].
Originally meant [[guinea fowl]], sold into Europe by Turkish traders, before the name moved to the North American bird.
Probably from an indigenous Peruvian language, Aymara or Quechua, reshaped to look like a Spanish diminutive ending in -illa.
A genuine diminutive, from Latin gerbillus, 'little jerboa'; ultimately from a Berber word, also found in Arabic, meaning 'flesh of the loins'.
Named after mice because muscles look like mice running under the skin; Jess compares this to [[gerbil]]'s 'flesh of the loins'.
Ultimately from a word meaning 'robber', as in Italian; English took it from French furet, which Rob links to fuir 'to flee'.
Originally meant sending your hunting [[ferret]] after something, not acting like a ferret; ferrets were domesticated to chase rabbits out of warrens.
The collective noun for [[ferret|ferrets]], a favourite term of the hosts.
An Australian term the hosts joke about; it leads them into [[budgerigar]].
From an unidentified Australian Aboriginal language: budgeri 'good' plus gar 'cockatoo'. Americans often call these birds [[parakeet|parakeets]].
From Middle French Perrot, a diminutive of Pierre used for someone who talks a lot or clippedly; related to [[parakeet]], with a parallel in [[robin]].
Related to [[parrot]]; possibly influenced by Italian parrochetto 'periwig', after the tufts of feathers on their heads, linking it to [[peruke]].
Lory, a Malay bird name, plus -keet from [[parakeet]], a [[cranberry morpheme]] from an Italian diminutive element.
A [[morpheme]] found in only one word, like cran in [[cranberry]], rasp in [[raspberry]] or boysen in boysenberry.
Cran comes from crane, because the flowers look like little crane heads; the classic [[cranberry morpheme]].
Its rasp is thought to be unrelated to the rasp of a sore throat, making it another [[cranberry morpheme]].
A unit of a word, a bit like a syllable but not quite.
Originally a diminutive of Robert, just as [[parrot]] comes from Pierrot, a cute form of Peter.
Pie was the bird's original name; mag, short for Margaret and an epithet for a chatty woman, was added because the birds are chatty.
Named after the Canary Islands, from Latin for 'island of dogs', so the bird is indirectly named after dogs.
A familiar human nickname for parrots, a variant of Molly or Mary; popularised by Andrew Jackson's parrot Poll, which swore loudly at his funeral.
A classic dog name meaning faithful or trustworthy, related to [[fidelity]].
A dog that roves and adventures; popularised by the 1905 British film Rescued by Rover, and similar in meaning to [[Ranger]].
Jess's long-legged dog, named in homage to Aragorn, the ranger nicknamed Longshanks in The Lord of the Rings.
A common cat name meaning happy or lucky, popular thanks to Felix the Cat and its likeness to Latin felis, source of [[feline]].
Justin Bieber's capuchin monkey, named after the rapper Mally Mall, who gave it to him.
